#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Secure FTPS (explicit TLS) deploy of dist/ via lftp.
#
# Usage:
#   scripts/deploy-ftp.sh            # dry run (shows what would change)
#   scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --apply    # upload for real
#   scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --apply --delete   # also remove remote files not in dist/
#
# Shows a single live-updating status line while running, then a summary of
# the files targeted for change. Asks for confirmation when not on master/main.
#
# Config (env vars, none are secrets except the password):
#   FTP_HOST        default: ftps4.us.freehostia.com
#   FTP_USER        REQUIRED, your FTP login (kept out of the repo on purpose)
#   FTP_REMOTE_DIR  REQUIRED, e.g. /public_html
#   FTP_PASS        optional; else read from macOS Keychain item "jcc-ftp",
#                   else prompted (hidden). Never put it in a file in the repo.
#
# One-time Keychain setup. -T "" trusts no app, so every read must be approved
# in a macOS dialog (choose "Allow", never "Always Allow"):
#   security delete-generic-password -a "$FTP_USER" -s jcc-ftp 2>/dev/null
#   security add-generic-password -a "$FTP_USER" -s jcc-ftp -T "" -w
#
# Security model:
#   - TLS is mandatory (ftp:ssl-force): lftp aborts before sending the
#     password if the server will not negotiate TLS or its certificate/hostname
#     fails verification. Run scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh to check this.
#   - Password reaches lftp only via LFTP_PASSWORD (open --env-password), so it
#     is not in argv, not in the lftp command text, and not in lftp's URLs.
#   - FTP_PASS is removed from the environment before `npm run build`.
#   - Any unrecognised lftp output is scrubbed of user:pass@ before printing.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

HOST="${FTP_HOST:-ftps4.us.freehostia.com}"
USER_NAME="${FTP_USER:?Set FTP_USER (your FTP login)}"
REMOTE_DIR="${FTP_REMOTE_DIR:?Set FTP_REMOTE_DIR (e.g. /public_html)}"

# Take the password out of the environment now, so the build's child
# processes (Astro, plugins, npm deps) never inherit it.
PASS="${FTP_PASS:-}"
unset FTP_PASS

APPLY=0
DELETE=0
for arg in "$@"; do
  case "$arg" in
    --apply) APPLY=1 ;;
    --delete) DELETE=1 ;;
    *) echo "Unknown arg: $arg" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done

command -v lftp >/dev/null || { echo "lftp missing: brew install lftp" >&2; exit 1; }

# --- Branch guard -----------------------------------------------------------
BRANCH="$(git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo unknown)"
if [ "$BRANCH" != "master" ] && [ "$BRANCH" != "main" ]; then
  echo "WARNING: on branch '$BRANCH', not master/main."
  echo "         The deployed site will be built from this branch."
  ans=""
  read -r -p "Continue anyway? [y/N] " ans || true
  case "$ans" in
    y|Y|yes|YES) ;;
    *) echo "Aborted."; exit 1 ;;
  esac
fi

# --- Temp files -------------------------------------------------------------
BUILD_LOG="$(mktemp)"
ACTIONS="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$BUILD_LOG" "$ACTIONS"' EXIT

# --- Live status line -------------------------------------------------------
if [ -t 1 ]; then
  TTY=1
  COLS="$(tput cols 2>/dev/null || echo 80)"
else
  TTY=0
  COLS=80
fi

# status "text": rewrite the current line (or plain line when not a TTY)
status() {
  if [ "$TTY" -eq 1 ]; then
    local s="$1"
    [ "${#s}" -ge "$COLS" ] && s="${s:0:$((COLS - 2))}…"
    printf '\r\033[K%s' "$s"
  else
    printf '%s\n' "$1"
  fi
}
# endstatus: clear the live line
endstatus() { [ "$TTY" -eq 1 ] && printf '\r\033[K' || true; }

# --- Build ------------------------------------------------------------------
status "Building site..."
if ! npm run build >"$BUILD_LOG" 2>&1; then
  endstatus
  echo "Build failed:" >&2
  tail -n 40 "$BUILD_LOG" >&2
  exit 1
fi
endstatus
echo "Build OK (branch: $BRANCH)"

[ -f dist/index.html ] || { echo "dist/index.html missing, aborting" >&2; exit 1; }

# --- Password: env (captured above) -> Keychain -> hidden prompt -------------
if [ -z "$PASS" ] && command -v security >/dev/null; then
  PASS="$(security find-generic-password -a "$USER_NAME" -s jcc-ftp -w 2>/dev/null || true)"
fi
if [ -z "$PASS" ]; then
  read -r -s -p "FTP password for $USER_NAME@$HOST: " PASS
  echo
fi

OPTS="--reverse --only-newer --parallel=2 --verbose"
[ "$DELETE" -eq 1 ] && OPTS="$OPTS --delete"
if [ "$APPLY" -eq 0 ]; then
  OPTS="$OPTS --dry-run"
  echo "DRY RUN (use --apply to upload)"
fi

# redact: strip credentials from any ftp(s)://user:pass@ URL in a line
redact() {
  printf '%s\n' "$1" | sed -E 's#(ftps?://[^/:@[:space:]]*):[^@[:space:]]*@#\1:***@#g'
}

# --- Run lftp, parse its output into live status + action list --------------
# The password is handed over in LFTP_PASSWORD (read by open --env-password);
# it is never part of argv, the lftp script text, or the session URL.
# `cd` before mirror forces login + TLS + path check up front, so a bad
# password or missing dir fails loudly instead of printing an empty plan.
# lftp verbose lines parsed:
#   Transferring file `X'      -> upload X
#   Removing old file `X'      -> remove X (before overwrite, or --delete)
#   Making directory `X'       -> mkdir X
#   Removing old directory `X' -> rmdir X
status "Connecting to $HOST..."
set +e
LFTP_PASSWORD="$PASS" lftp <<EOF 2>&1 | while IFS= read -r line; do
set cmd:fail-exit yes
set ftp:ssl-allow yes
set ftp:ssl-force yes
set ftp:ssl-auth TLS
set ftp:ssl-protect-data yes
set ftp:ssl-protect-list yes
set ssl:verify-certificate yes
set ssl:check-hostname yes
set ftp:sync-mode yes
set net:max-retries 2
set net:timeout 20
open --env-password -u "$USER_NAME" ftp://$HOST
cd "$REMOTE_DIR"
mirror $OPTS --exclude-glob .DS_Store dist/ .
bye
EOF
  case "$line" in
    "Transferring file \`"*)
      f="${line#*\`}"; f="${f%\'}"
      printf 'T\t%s\n' "$f" >>"$ACTIONS"
      status "$([ "$APPLY" -eq 1 ] && echo Uploading || echo Checking): $f" ;;
    "Removing old file \`"*)
      f="${line#*\`}"; f="${f%\'}"
      printf 'R\t%s\n' "$f" >>"$ACTIONS"
      status "Replacing: $f" ;;
    "Making directory \`"*)
      f="${line#*\`}"; f="${f%\'}"
      printf 'M\t%s\n' "$f" >>"$ACTIONS"
      status "Creating dir: $f" ;;
    "Removing old directory \`"*)
      f="${line#*\`}"; f="${f%\'}"
      printf 'X\t%s\n' "$f" >>"$ACTIONS"
      status "Removing dir: $f" ;;
    # dry-run echoes the underlying commands; ignore that noise
    "get "*|"put "*|"rm "*|"rmdir "*|"mkdir "*|"chmod "*|"") ;;
    *)
      endstatus
      redact "$line" >&2 ;;
  esac
done
RC="${PIPESTATUS[0]}"
set -e
endstatus

if [ "$RC" -ne 0 ]; then
  echo "lftp failed (exit $RC). Check output above." >&2
  exit "$RC"
fi

# --- Summary ----------------------------------------------------------------
# A file with both R and T = overwritten; T only = new; R only = deleted.
awk -F'\t' -v apply="$APPLY" '
  $1=="T" { t[$2]=1; order[++n]=$2 }
  $1=="R" { r[$2]=1; if (!($2 in seen)) { seen[$2]=1; rorder[++m]=$2 } }
  $1=="M" { dirs[++d]=$2 }
  $1=="X" { rdirs[++x]=$2 }
  END {
    for (i=1;i<=n;i++) { f=order[i]; if (f in r) upd[++u]=f; else new[++w]=f }
    for (i=1;i<=m;i++) { f=rorder[i]; if (!(f in t)) del[++k]=f }
    verb = apply ? "Changed" : "Would change"
    print ""
    print "== " verb ": " u+0 " updated, " w+0 " new, " k+0 " deleted, " d+0 " dirs created, " x+0 " dirs removed =="
    cap=100
    sec("Updated", upd, u, cap, "~")
    sec("New", new, w, cap, "+")
    sec("Deleted", del, k, cap, "-")
    sec("Dirs created", dirs, d, cap, "+")
    sec("Dirs removed", rdirs, x, cap, "-")
    if (u+w+k+d+x == 0) print "Nothing to do: remote already up to date."
  }
  function sec(title, arr, cnt, cap, mark,   i) {
    if (cnt+0 == 0) return
    print title " (" cnt "):"
    for (i=1;i<=cnt && i<=cap;i++) print "  " mark " " arr[i]
    if (cnt > cap) print "  ... and " (cnt-cap) " more"
  }
' "$ACTIONS"

[ "$APPLY" -eq 0 ] && echo && echo "Dry run only. Re-run with --apply to upload."
exit 0

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Offline regression test for scripts/deploy-ftp.sh security guarantees.
# Runs the real deploy script against a local fake FTP server (no network,
# no real credentials) and asserts that the password is never sent or printed:
#
#   1. Server without TLS          -> script aborts, server never sees USER/PASS
#   2. Server with untrusted cert  -> script aborts, server never sees PASS
#      (lftp checks the cert right after the handshake, so USER may already
#      have gone out inside TLS; the username is not secret, the password is)
#
# Usage: scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh      (needs python3, lftp, openssl, dist/)
set -uo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

[ -f dist/index.html ] || { echo "Run 'npm run build' once first (dist/ missing)." >&2; exit 2; }
for bin in python3 lftp openssl; do
  command -v "$bin" >/dev/null || { echo "Missing: $bin" >&2; exit 2; }
done

WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
SRV_PID=""
cleanup() { [ -n "$SRV_PID" ] && kill "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null; rm -rf "$WORK"; }
trap cleanup EXIT

FAKE_PW="REDACTED"   # fake value; must never show up anywhere

# Stub npm so the test does not rebuild the site.
mkdir -p "$WORK/bin"
printf '#!/bin/sh\nexit 0\n' >"$WORK/bin/npm"
chmod +x "$WORK/bin/npm"

# Self-signed cert for test 2 (not trusted by the system CA store).
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -days 1 -subj "/CN=127.0.0.1" \
  -keyout "$WORK/key.pem" -out "$WORK/cert.pem" >/dev/null 2>&1

cat >"$WORK/fakeftp.py" <<'PY'
import socket, ssl, sys
mode, portfile, logfile, certdir = sys.argv[1:5]
log = open(logfile, "a", buffering=1)
srv = socket.socket()
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
srv.listen(4)
srv.settimeout(20)
open(portfile, "w").write(str(srv.getsockname()[1]))
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
ctx.load_cert_chain(certdir + "/cert.pem", certdir + "/key.pem")
while True:
    try:
        conn, _ = srv.accept()
    except socket.timeout:
        break
    conn.settimeout(10)
    f = conn.makefile("rwb", buffering=0)
    send = lambda s: f.write((s + "\r\n").encode())
    send("220 fake")
    try:
        while True:
            line = f.readline()
            if not line:
                break
            cmd = line.decode(errors="replace").strip()
            log.write("C: " + cmd + "\n")
            verb = cmd.split(" ")[0].upper()
            if verb == "FEAT":
                f.write(b"211-Features:\r\n AUTH TLS\r\n PBSZ\r\n PROT\r\n211 End\r\n")
            elif verb == "AUTH" and mode == "notls":
                send("534 TLS refused")
            elif verb == "AUTH" and mode == "selfsigned":
                send("234 go ahead")
                try:
                    conn = ctx.wrap_socket(conn, server_side=True)
                    f = conn.makefile("rwb", buffering=0)
                    send = lambda s: f.write((s + "\r\n").encode())
                    log.write("TLS handshake completed\n")
                except Exception as e:
                    log.write("TLS handshake rejected by client: %s\n" % e)
                    break
            elif verb == "USER":
                send("331 need password")
            elif verb == "PASS":
                send("530 login incorrect")
            elif verb == "QUIT":
                send("221 bye")
                break
            else:
                send("502 not implemented")
    except Exception:
        pass
    conn.close()
PY

FAILS=0
check() { # check "description" condition-exit-code
  if [ "$2" -eq 0 ]; then echo "  PASS  $1"; else echo "  FAIL  $1"; FAILS=$((FAILS + 1)); fi
}

run_case() { # run_case mode title forbidden-commands-regex
  local mode="$1" title="$2" forbidden="$3"
  local portfile="$WORK/port.$mode" srvlog="$WORK/srv.$mode.log" out="$WORK/out.$mode.log"
  : >"$srvlog"
  python3 -I "$WORK/fakeftp.py" "$mode" "$portfile" "$srvlog" "$WORK" &
  SRV_PID=$!
  for _ in $(seq 50); do [ -s "$portfile" ] && break; sleep 0.1; done
  local port; port="$(cat "$portfile")"

  echo "== $title"
  # "y" answers the branch guard if not on master/main.
  echo y | PATH="$WORK/bin:$PATH" FTP_HOST="127.0.0.1:$port" FTP_USER=testuser \
    FTP_PASS="$FAKE_PW" FTP_REMOTE_DIR=/www scripts/deploy-ftp.sh >"$out" 2>&1
  local rc=$?
  kill "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null; wait "$SRV_PID" 2>/dev/null; SRV_PID=""

  [ "$rc" -ne 0 ];                                  check "deploy script exits non-zero (rc=$rc)" $?
  grep -q '^C: AUTH TLS' "$srvlog";                 check "client asked for TLS (AUTH TLS)" $?
  ! grep -qE "^C: ($forbidden)" "$srvlog";          check "server never received ${forbidden//|//}" $?
  ! grep -qF "$FAKE_PW" "$srvlog" "$out";           check "password not in server log or script output" $?
  if [ "$FAILS" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "  --- server log:";  sed 's/^/    /' "$srvlog"
    echo "  --- script output:"; sed 's/^/    /' "$out"
  fi
}

run_case notls      "Server refuses TLS"                       'USER|PASS'
run_case selfsigned "Server presents an untrusted certificate" 'PASS'

echo
if [ "$FAILS" -eq 0 ]; then echo "All checks passed."; else echo "$FAILS check(s) FAILED."; exit 1; fi

# Deployment Guide

This guide explains how to deploy the Jyväskylä Cricket Club website.

## Recommended: Netlify Deployment

### Prerequisites
- A GitHub repository with this code
- A Netlify account (free tier is sufficient)

### Steps

1. **Push code to GitHub**
   ```bash
   git add .
   git commit -m "Modernized JCC website with Astro"
   git push origin main
   ```

2. **Connect to Netlify**
   - Go to [https://app.netlify.com](https://app.netlify.com)
   - Click "Add new site" → "Import an existing project"
   - Choose GitHub and select your repository
   - Netlify will auto-detect the Astro framework

3. **Configure Build Settings** (should be auto-detected)
   - Build command: `npm run build`
   - Publish directory: `dist`
   - Node version: 22

4. **Deploy!**
   - Click "Deploy site"
   - Netlify will build and deploy your site
   - You'll get a temporary URL like `random-name.netlify.app`

5. **Custom Domain Setup**
   - Go to Site settings → Domain management
   - Add custom domain: `cricketjyvaskyla.com`
   - Follow DNS configuration instructions
   - Netlify provides free SSL certificates

### Auto-Deploy
After initial setup, every push to `main` branch will automatically:
- Build the site
- Run checks
- Deploy if successful

## Alternative: Vercel Deployment

Similar to Netlify:
1. Go to [https://vercel.com](https://vercel.com)
2. Import your GitHub repository
3. Vercel auto-detects Astro
4. Deploy!

## Alternative: Traditional Hosting

If using traditional hosting (FTP/cPanel):

1. **Build the site locally**
   ```bash
   npm run build
   ```

2. **Upload the `dist/` folder**
   - The `dist/` folder contains all static files
   - Upload contents to your web server's public directory
   - Usually `public_html/` or `www/`

3. **Important**:
   - Ensure PDF files in `dist/pdfs/` are uploaded
   - Check that `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` are in root

### Secured upload script (FTPS)

`scripts/deploy-ftp.sh` builds the site and mirrors `dist/` over FTP with mandatory TLS (explicit FTPS, via lftp). It never sends the password unless TLS is negotiated and the server certificate and hostname verify.

One-time setup (macOS):

```bash
brew install lftp
export FTP_USER=<your-ftp-login>
# Store the password in the Keychain. -T "" makes every read ask for approval
# (choose "Allow", never "Always Allow").
security add-generic-password -a "$FTP_USER" -s jcc-ftp -T "" -w
```

Usage:

```bash
export FTP_USER=<your-ftp-login>
export FTP_REMOTE_DIR=/<web-root>      # folder that holds the live site
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh                  # dry run: summary of files that would change
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --apply          # upload
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --apply --delete # also delete remote files not in dist/
```

- Host defaults to `ftps4.us.freehostia.com` (override with `FTP_HOST`).
- Asks for confirmation when not run from `master`.
- Run it in your own terminal, not through an AI agent's shell, so the session transcript never contains deploy output.
- `scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh` is an offline regression test against a fake FTP server: it checks the password is never sent when the server refuses TLS or presents an untrusted certificate. Run it after changing the deploy script.
- FileZilla: use host `ftps4.us.freehostia.com` with "Require explicit FTP over TLS". Plain FTP sends the password unencrypted.

## Environment Variables

No environment variables needed for basic deployment. All configuration is in `astro.config.mjs`.

## Post-Deployment Checklist

- [ ] Site loads at custom domain
- [ ] All 8 pages are accessible
- [ ] Images load correctly
- [ ] PDFs download properly
- [ ] Navigation works on mobile
- [ ] SSL certificate active (HTTPS)
- [ ] robots.txt accessible at `/robots.txt`
- [ ] sitemap.xml accessible at `/sitemap.xml`
- [ ] Old URLs redirect to new ones (e.g., `/members.html` → `/members`)

## Monitoring

- **Netlify**: Built-in analytics available
- **Google Search Console**: Add your domain for SEO monitoring
- **Google Analytics**: Add tracking code if needed

## Rollback

If you need to rollback:
- **Netlify**: Go to Deploys → select previous deploy → "Publish deploy"
- **Vercel**: Similar rollback in deployments section

## Support

For issues:
- Netlify docs: https://docs.netlify.com
- Astro docs: https://docs.astro.build
- Contact: chairman@cricketjyvaskyla.com

content.text:
I fixed five of the seven findings and dismissed two that didn't hold up. The fixes are pushed as `927259d` on PR #10. CI `build` passes, and Entire's Code review and Slop reviewers are re-running on the new commit.

Some findings were guesses about lftp's behaviour, so I tested each one against lftp 4.9.3 and a fake FTPS server I built (encrypted login and file transfers, a throwaway certificate) before acting on it.

| Finding | What I found | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| **High:** "a dry run never prints `Transferring file`, so the summary always says nothing to do" | Not true. A dry run against an FTP server prints those lines, so the summary is correct. | Dismissed, with the evidence attached |
| Medium: "`Removing old file` only appears with `--delete`" | Not true. It also appears when an existing file is overwritten. | Dismissed, with the evidence attached |
| Medium: the server rejects `PROT P` (encrypted file transfers) | **Real and serious.** lftp kept going and uploaded every file unencrypted. | Fixed |
| Medium: a non-English locale breaks the summary | **Real.** Under German, lftp prints `Sende Datei »…«` and the parser misses it. | Fixed |
| Medium: every build re-uploads the whole site | **Real.** All 121 files (20 MB) were sent every run, because each build gives every file a new timestamp. | Fixed |
| Medium: the test only covers refusals | **Real.** | Fixed |
| Low: wrong test labels and a failure counter that never reset | Real. | Fixed |

How each one was fixed:
- **Unencrypted transfers:** a quick check now logs in first and stops if the server didn't accept `PROT P`. lftp asks for it during login, so nothing is listed or uploaded before the check. It also catches a wrong password or folder before anything else happens.
- **Locale:** lftp now always prints English messages. UTF-8 file names like `jyväskylä.txt` still transfer correctly.
- **Re-uploads:** a new helper, `scripts/deploy-ftp-state.mjs`, records a fingerprint of each file after a successful upload. Before the next run it restores the old timestamp on files that haven't changed, so only real changes go up. I didn't compare by file size instead, because that misses same-length edits like Abhiskek → Abhishek. A new `--full` flag re-uploads everything if the server was changed some other way, such as through FileZilla.
- **Test:** `scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh` now runs the real script end to end against `scripts/fake_ftps_server.py`.
  - It covers 4 refusal cases: no TLS, untrusted certificate, `PROT P` rejected, wrong password.
  - It covers 7 success cases: dry run, `--delete`, apply, rebuild with nothing changed, one file changed, German locale, `--full`.
  - It passed three runs in a row. I also broke each fix on purpose in a copy of the script, and the test failed every time.

While building the fake server I hit a bug in the fake server itself (TLS session tickets in Python), not in the deploy script, and fixed it there.

I marked the five fixed findings resolved and the two false positives dismissed, each with its evidence. Reopen either dismissal if you disagree. `DEPLOYMENT.md` and the PR description are updated.

The re-review on `927259d` may raise new findings; I can pull and fix those once it finishes. Before your real upload, run `export FTP_USER=aksgul5` and set `FTP_REMOTE_DIR` to the correct folder.

# Requesting Code Review

Dispatch a code reviewer subagent to catch issues before they cascade. The reviewer gets precisely crafted context for evaluation — never your session's history.

**Core principle:** Review early, review often.

## When to Request Review

**Mandatory:**
- After each task in subagent-driven development
- After completing major feature
- Before merge to main

**Optional but valuable:**
- When stuck (fresh perspective)
- Before refactoring (baseline check)
- After fixing complex bug

## How to Request

**1. Get git SHAs:**
```bash
BASE_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD~1)  # or: git merge-base origin/main HEAD
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
```

**2. Dispatch code reviewer subagent:**

Dispatch a `general-purpose` subagent, filling the template at [code-reviewer.md](code-reviewer.md)

**Placeholders:**
- `{DESCRIPTION}` - Brief summary of what you built
- `{PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS}` - What it should do
- `{BASE_SHA}` - Starting commit
- `{HEAD_SHA}` - Ending commit

**3. Act on feedback:**
- Fix Critical issues immediately
- Fix Important issues before proceeding
- Note Minor issues for later
- Push back if reviewer is wrong (with reasoning)

## Example

```
[Just completed Task 2: Add verification function]

You: Let me request code review before proceeding.

BASE_SHA=$(git log --oneline | grep "Task 1" | head -1 | cut -d' ' -f1)
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

[Dispatch code reviewer subagent]
  DESCRIPTION: Added verifyIndex() and repairIndex() with 4 issue types
  PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS: Task 2 from docs/superpowers/plans/deployment-plan.md
  BASE_SHA: a7981ec
  HEAD_SHA: 3df7661

[Subagent returns]:
  Strengths: Clean architecture, real tests
  Issues:
    Important: Missing progress indicators
    Minor: Magic number (100) for reporting interval
  Assessment: Ready to proceed

You: [Fix progress indicators]
[Continue to Task 3]
```

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I'll just review the diff myself instead of dispatching a reviewer" | You're the coordinator — reviewing the diff inline burns the context window you need to keep driving the work. Dispatch a reviewer subagent: the diff and the evaluation live in its context, and only the findings come back to you. |
| "The reviewer needs my whole session history to understand the change" | Hand it precisely crafted context, never your session's history. That keeps the reviewer on the work product, not your thought process. |

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Skip review because "it's simple"
- Ignore Critical issues
- Proceed with unfixed Important issues
- Argue with valid technical feedback

**If reviewer wrong:**
- Push back with technical reasoning
- Show code/tests that prove it works
- Request clarification

See template at: [code-reviewer.md](code-reviewer.md)

33	    ## The spec is a vision document
34	
35	    The spec says what the software must do. It does not enumerate every
36	    input, environment, or condition the software will meet. For behavior
37	    the spec is silent on, judge by what a reasonable person using this
38	    software would expect: a reasonable person's expectation is a
39	    requirement, and a spec's silence is not permission. Grade such
40	    findings by their effect on that person, not by whether the spec

52	    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way. Use tools like `git show`, `git diff`, and `git log` to inspect history. If you need a working copy of a different revision, check it out into a separate temporary directory (e.g. `git worktree add /tmp/review-[SHA] [SHA]`) — never move HEAD on this checkout.

57	    of the diff, and never spawn another reviewer for a second opinion.
58	    This process already provides every review seat the work gets; a
59	    reviewer you spawn duplicates one of them at full cost, and its

# Code Reviewer Prompt Template

Use this template when dispatching a code reviewer subagent.

**Purpose:** Review completed work against requirements and code quality standards before it cascades into more work.

```
Subagent (general-purpose):
  description: "Review code changes"
  prompt: |
    You are a Senior Code Reviewer with expertise in software architecture,
    design patterns, and best practices. Your job is to review completed work
    against its plan or requirements and identify issues before they cascade.

    ## What Was Implemented

    [DESCRIPTION]

    ## Requirements / Plan

    [PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS]

    ## Git Range to Review

    **Base:** [BASE_SHA]
    **Head:** [HEAD_SHA]

    ```bash
    git diff --stat [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
    git diff [BASE_SHA]..[HEAD_SHA]
    ```

    ## The spec is a vision document

    The spec says what the software must do. It does not enumerate every
    input, environment, or condition the software will meet. For behavior
    the spec is silent on, judge by what a reasonable person using this
    software would expect: a reasonable person's expectation is a
    requirement, and a spec's silence is not permission. Grade such
    findings by their effect on that person, not by whether the spec
    mentions the trigger.

    ## Declined to judge

    Before your verdict, list every behavior you considered and set aside
    as outside the plan or spec, one line each, with the reason. The
    executor rules on each line; nothing you set aside is dropped
    silently. An empty list means you set nothing aside.

    ## Read-Only Review

    Your review is read-only on this checkout. Do not mutate the working tree, the index, HEAD, or branch state in any way. Use tools like `git show`, `git diff`, and `git log` to inspect history. If you need a working copy of a different revision, check it out into a separate temporary directory (e.g. `git worktree add /tmp/review-[SHA] [SHA]`) — never move HEAD on this checkout.

    ## You Do Not Dispatch Subagents

    Do all of this review yourself. Never spawn a subagent to review part
    of the diff, and never spawn another reviewer for a second opinion.
    This process already provides every review seat the work gets; a
    reviewer you spawn duplicates one of them at full cost, and its
    verdict counts for nothing. If the diff feels too large for one
    pass, review it in passes yourself and say so in your report.

    ## What to Check

    **Plan alignment:**
    - Does the implementation match the plan / requirements?
    - Are deviations justified improvements, or problematic departures?
    - Is all planned functionality present?

    **Code quality:**
    - Clean separation of concerns?
    - Proper error handling?
    - Type safety where applicable?
    - DRY without premature abstraction?
    - Edge cases handled?

    **Architecture:**
    - Sound design decisions?
    - Reasonable scalability and performance?
    - Security concerns?
    - Integrates cleanly with surrounding code?

    **Testing:**
    - Tests verify real behavior, not mocks?
    - Edge cases covered?
    - Integration tests where they matter?
    - All tests passing?

    **Production readiness:**
    - Migration strategy if schema changed?
    - Backward compatibility considered?
    - Documentation complete?
    - No obvious bugs?

    ## Calibration

    Categorize issues by actual severity. Not everything is Critical.
    Acknowledge what was done well before listing issues — accurate praise
    helps the implementer trust the rest of the feedback.

    If you find significant deviations from the plan, flag them specifically
    so the implementer can confirm whether the deviation was intentional.
    If you find issues with the plan itself rather than the implementation,
    say so.

    ## Output Format

    ### Strengths
    [What's well done? Be specific.]

    ### Issues

    #### Critical (Must Fix)
    [Bugs, security issues, data loss risks, broken functionality]

    #### Important (Should Fix)
    [Architecture problems, missing features, poor error handling, test gaps]

    #### Minor (Nice to Have)
    [Code style, optimization opportunities, documentation polish]

    For each issue:
    - File:line reference
    - What's wrong
    - Why it matters
    - How to fix (if not obvious)

    ### Recommendations
    [Improvements for code quality, architecture, or process]

    ### Assessment

    **Ready to merge?** [Yes | No | With fixes]

    **Reasoning:** [1-2 sentence technical assessment]

    ## Critical Rules

    **DO:**
    - Categorize by actual severity
    - Be specific (file:line, not vague)
    - Explain WHY each issue matters
    - Acknowledge strengths
    - Give a clear verdict

    **DON'T:**
    - Say "looks good" without checking
    - Mark nitpicks as Critical
    - Give feedback on code you didn't actually read
    - Be vague ("improve error handling")
    - Avoid giving a clear verdict
```

**Placeholders:**
- `[DESCRIPTION]` — brief summary of what was built
- `[PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS]` — what it should do (plan file path, task text, or requirements)
- `[BASE_SHA]` — starting commit
- `[HEAD_SHA]` — ending commit

**Reviewer returns:** Strengths, Issues (Critical / Important / Minor), Recommendations, Assessment

## Example Output

```
### Strengths
- Clean database schema with proper migrations (db.ts:15-42)
- Comprehensive test coverage (18 tests, all edge cases)
- Good error handling with fallbacks (summarizer.ts:85-92)

### Issues

#### Important
1. **Missing help text in CLI wrapper**
   - File: index-conversations:1-31
   - Issue: No --help flag, users won't discover --concurrency
   - Fix: Add --help case with usage examples

2. **Date validation missing**
   - File: search.ts:25-27

#### Minor
1. **Progress indicators**

### Recommendations
- Add progress reporting for user experience

### Assessment

**Ready to merge: With fixes**

**Reasoning:** Core implementation is solid with good architecture and tests. Important issues (help text, date validation) are easily fixed and don't affect core functionality.
```

input.prompt:
You are a Senior Code Reviewer with expertise in software architecture, design patterns, and best practices. Your job is to review completed work against its plan or requirements and identify issues before they cascade.

Repository: /Users/akshay.guleria/work/cricketjyvaskyla (Astro 7 static website for a cricket club; see CLAUDE.md there for repo conventions — note CRLF line endings in DEPLOYMENT.md, root-relative links, etc.).

## What Was Implemented

A secured FTPS deploy path for the static site (an alternative to the existing Netlify deploy), on branch `feat/secure-ftp-deploy`, two commits:
- `scripts/deploy-ftp.sh` — builds the site (`npm run build`), then mirrors `dist/` to a shared web host (Freehostia, `ftps4.us.freehostia.com`) using lftp 4.9.3 over explicit FTPS. Dry run by default; `--apply` uploads; `--delete` removes remote files not in dist/; `--full` ignores the incremental record. Shows a single live-updating status line, then a summary (updated/new/deleted files, dirs created/removed) parsed from lftp's English verbose output. Branch guard asks for confirmation off master/main. Password from FTP_PASS (captured then unset before the build), macOS Keychain item `jcc-ftp`, or hidden prompt; handed to lftp only via `LFTP_PASSWORD` + `open --env-password`. TLS mandatory (`ftp:ssl-allow yes`, `ftp:ssl-force yes`, cert + hostname verification, `ftp:sync-mode yes`). A preflight lftp session (login + `cd` only, debug log on with password masked) checks every `PROT P` reply was 2xx before the real mirror session runs (lftp 4.9.3 silently falls back to cleartext data connections when PROT P is rejected). lftp runs with `LC_ALL=` `LANGUAGE=` `LC_MESSAGES=C` and the user's LC_CTYPE so the parser sees English messages. Unrecognised lftp output is scrubbed of `user:pass@`.

  ## Review: `feat/secure-ftp-deploy` (493ac5c..927259d)
  
  **Verdict: Ready to merge with fixes.** The happy path is solid and well tested. I found four real problems, all reproduced against a modified fake server. Two are on the failure path and can leave the live site wrong. Two are gaps in the security promises.
  
  I ran `scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh` six times. Every run passed in about 3 s, so I saw no flakiness. Disabling the PROT P refusal makes 3 checks fail, so the suite does catch that regression. For the experiments I used copies of the scripts plus a modified fake server, all in the scratchpad (`.../scratchpad/exp/`). The server's new modes are: PROT P accepted only on the first connection, a STOR that fails or runs slowly on demand, a server that ignores SITE UTIME, and a server that rejects SITE CHMOD. Nothing in the repo was changed, no real host was contacted, and no stray processes are left.
  
  ### Strengths
  - **Password handling is sound:**
    - `FTP_PASS` is copied and unset before the build.
    - The password reaches lftp only through `LFTP_PASSWORD` with `--env-password`, never in argv.
    - The Keychain item uses `-T ""`, and the fallback prompt is hidden.
    - The password never appeared in output, the server log, or lftp's debug logs (shown as `PASS XXXX`).
  - **TLS fails closed.** If the server refuses TLS, the certificate is untrusted, or the password is wrong, nothing is uploaded. In the first two cases the password is never sent.
  - **The PROT P preflight fails closed.** It needs at least one PROT P and every reply 2xx. It reliably catches a server that is consistently misconfigured.
  - **The manifest is handled safely.** It is written atomically. A corrupt or missing manifest just means a full upload. It lives under `node_modules/.cache`, so wiping that folder is also safe.
  - **The test suite is good:**
    - The fake server listens on localhost only, uses an ephemeral port (no port races) and a throwaway CA, and tags every command and data connection with `tls=`.
    - The tests check the real server state, not mocks.
  - **Ctrl-C is handled cleanly** (verified with SIGINT reset to default): exit 130, lftp is gone, all temp files including the debug log are removed, and the manifest is not saved.
  - **Other points:**
    - The defaults are safe: dry run unless `--apply`, deletes only with `--delete`, and the branch guard aborts if it gets no answer.
    - Messages stay in English while UTF-8 file names still work.
    - The scripts run on macOS bash 3.2.
    - DEPLOYMENT.md keeps CRLF on all 35 added lines.
    - No secrets or login are committed.
  
  ### Critical
  None.
  
  ### Important
  
  **I1. A failed or interrupted `--apply` deletes live files** (`scripts/deploy-ftp.sh:200`). Verified.
  - Without `--overwrite`, lftp deletes each file on the server before uploading the new one (DELE, then STOR).
  - When I made the server fail the `site.css` upload, the server ended up with no `site.css` at all.
  - When I pressed Ctrl-C partway through, `index.html` and `about.html` were left missing, so the homepage would 404.

**Verdict: Ready to merge with fixes.** The happy path is solid and well tested. I found four real problems, all reproduced against a modified fake server. Two are on the failure path and can leave the live site wrong. Two are gaps in the security promises.

I ran `scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh` six times. Every run passed in about 3 s, so I saw no flakiness. Disabling the PROT P refusal makes 3 checks fail, so the suite does catch that regression. For the experiments I used copies of the scripts plus a modified fake server, all in the scratchpad (`.../scratchpad/exp/`). The server's new modes are: PROT P accepted only on the first connection, a STOR that fails or runs slowly on demand, a server that ignores SITE UTIME, and a server that rejects SITE CHMOD. Nothing in the repo was changed, no real host was contacted, and no stray processes are left.

### Strengths
- **Password handling is sound:**
  - `FTP_PASS` is copied and unset before the build.
  - The password reaches lftp only through `LFTP_PASSWORD` with `--env-password`, never in argv.
  - The Keychain item uses `-T ""`, and the fallback prompt is hidden.
  - The password never appeared in output, the server log, or lftp's debug logs (shown as `PASS XXXX`).
- **TLS fails closed.** If the server refuses TLS, the certificate is untrusted, or the password is wrong, nothing is uploaded. In the first two cases the password is never sent.
- **The PROT P preflight fails closed.** It needs at least one PROT P and every reply 2xx. It reliably catches a server that is consistently misconfigured.
- **The manifest is handled safely.** It is written atomically. A corrupt or missing manifest just means a full upload. It lives under `node_modules/.cache`, so wiping that folder is also safe.
- **The test suite is good:**
  - The fake server listens on localhost only, uses an ephemeral port (no port races) and a throwaway CA, and tags every command and data connection with `tls=`.
  - The tests check the real server state, not mocks.
- **Ctrl-C is handled cleanly** (verified with SIGINT reset to default): exit 130, lftp is gone, all temp files including the debug log are removed, and the manifest is not saved.
- **Other points:**
  - The defaults are safe: dry run unless `--apply`, deletes only with `--delete`, and the branch guard aborts if it gets no answer.
  - Messages stay in English while UTF-8 file names still work.
  - The scripts run on macOS bash 3.2.
  - DEPLOYMENT.md keeps CRLF on all 35 added lines.
  - No secrets or login are committed.

### Critical
None.

### Important

**I1. A failed or interrupted `--apply` deletes live files** (`scripts/deploy-ftp.sh:200`). Verified.
- Without `--overwrite`, lftp deletes each file on the server before uploading the new one (DELE, then STOR).
- When I made the server fail the `site.css` upload, the server ended up with no `site.css` at all.
- When I pressed Ctrl-C partway through, `index.html` and `about.html` were left missing, so the homepage would 404.
- The script only prints "lftp failed". Re-running fixes it, but if the cause persists (for example a full quota), each re-run deletes and fails again.
- **Fix:** add `--overwrite`, and add a parser case for `Overwriting old file \`X'`. Without that case the summary reports every update as "new". I verified that the old file survives a failed upload with this change.
- A stronger option is `set xfer:use-temp-file yes`, which uploads to `.in.X` and then renames. It also kept the old file. It needs the host to allow renaming over an existing file, and it prints no replace line, so the summary needs `--overwrite` alongside it.

**I2. Entire finding (a) is real, Important severity: the manifest goes stale after a failed or interrupted deploy** (`deploy-ftp.sh:136`, `:258-261`; `deploy-ftp-state.mjs:35-55`). Verified.
- Sequence: deploy A, then deploy B where `index.html` uploads and `site.css` fails, then roll back to A.
- On the rollback, `restore` puts back A's old timestamp, the server's copy is newer, and `--only-newer` skips the file.
- Result: "rc=0 … 0 updated", while B's `index.html` stays live.
- The same thing happens after Ctrl-C or kill -9, with a second computer that has its own manifest, and with edits made on the server directly.
- Dropping `--only-newer` alone is not enough. lftp's default upload rule keeps a newer server file unless the size differs, so a same-size change is still skipped (verified).
- Adding `--upload-older` fixes that, but on a server that ignores SITE UTIME it re-uploads everything on every deploy (verified: 3 uploads on a no-op rebuild).
- **Fix that works on both server types** (verified): before the live mirror, have `restore` write back a manifest with only the entries whose hash still matches. Simpler: delete the manifest when `APPLY=1`, at the cost of one full upload after any failure. I tested the delete version: the rollback re-uploads A on both server types.
- Also document that `--full` is needed after deploying from another computer.

**I3. Entire finding (b) is real: PROT P is only checked on the preflight connection** (`deploy-ftp.sh:166-198` vs `:217-224`). Verified.
- With a server that accepts PROT P on the first connection only, the preflight passed.
- Every mirror listing and upload then went over cleartext data connections (`DATA STOR … tls=0`).
- The script still printed "TLS OK: login and data connections encrypted" and exited 0.
- Likelihood is low: the verified server itself has to behave inconsistently. The impact is integrity, not confidentiality, because the site is public: an on-path attacker could tamper with uploaded files.
- lftp 4.9.3 has no setting that makes a refused PROT P fatal. It just re-sends PROT P before each transfer.
- **Fix (prototype verified):** add `debug -o "$MIRROR_DEBUG" 9` to the mirror session, then run the audit after lftp exits. On failure, exit non-zero, skip saving the manifest, and tell the user to check the site.
  - In my prototype the audit passed on the normal server and flagged the bad one (exit 3). The password was not in the log.
  - With `--parallel=2` the replies from different connections interleave, and `debug -c` tags lines only by hostname, so pairing each PROT P with its reply is unreliable. Use a count rule instead: the number of `---> PROT P` lines must equal the number of `---> PASS` lines (5 vs 2 in the bad case).
  - Also reword the line-198 message to say only that the server accepted PROT P, and add this server mode to the test suite.

- A leftover `set ssl:verify-certificate/localhost no` in the user's lftp rc file beats the script's `set ssl:verify-certificate yes`.
- Result: rc=0, the password was sent three times, and four files were uploaded to an untrusted certificate, all under "TLS OK".
- This is not live on your machine (no user rc file exists), but anyone else in the club who runs the script could have one.
- **Fix:** run lftp with `--norc`, which I verified skips the user rc. The test suite currently trusts its CA through `$LFTP_HOME/rc`, so give it a test-only way to pass the CA file instead. Re-setting each host-specific setting is weaker, because wildcard entries such as `/*.example.com` survive it.

- **M2:** if the server rejects SITE CHMOD, every `--apply` exits 1 and the manifest is never saved (verified with the fake server). Whether your host allows it is unknown. `--no-perms` would avoid the dependency.
- **M3** (`:201`, inferred): `--delete` has no protection for server-managed files (`.htaccess`, `.well-known/`, `cgi-bin`, `.ftpquota`), or for `FTP_REMOTE_DIR=/`. The dry run does show them first.
- **M4** (`:115`, inferred): `redact()` stops at the first `@`, so a password containing `@` would be only partly masked. This is defence in depth only; lftp never printed the password in my runs.
- **M5:** test gaps:
  - There are no cases for a partial failure followed by a rollback, PROT P refused on a later connection, Ctrl-C, or a server that ignores UTIME.
  - `start_server` (`test-deploy-ftp.sh:84-85`) doesn't stop with a clear error if the server never writes its port.
  - Linux was not exercised.
- **M6:** the "data connections encrypted" message overclaims (see I3).
- **M7** (DEPLOYMENT.md:99): "only files whose content changed … are uploaded" holds only on the happy path. Document `--full` after a failed or interrupted run, or when deploying from more than one computer.
- **M8** (inferred): on a server that ignores UTIME and whose clock runs ahead, `--only-newer` can skip files changed shortly after the last upload. lftp also compares at 1-second precision.

### Recommendations
1. Fix in this order: I1, then I2 (prune the manifest before uploading), then I3, then I4. Each is a few lines.
2. Add test cases to the fake server and suite for I1, I2 and I3; the server modes I used in the scratchpad can serve as templates.

- The branch guard not checking for uncommitted or unpushed changes: the spec scopes the guard to the branch only.

# FTPS deploy: fix plan for the review findings (waiting for your go-ahead)

Two reviews ran on commit `927259d`:
- **Entire's re-review:** 1 new open finding (medium).
- **A separate code review of the whole branch:**
  - Verdict "ready to merge with fixes": 0 critical, 4 important, 8 minor.
  - It confirmed both of Entire's points.
  - It reproduced each important issue against a modified copy of the fake server.

## What the reviews found

| # | Issue | My view |
|---|---|---|
| **I1** | When lftp replaces a file, it deletes the server copy first, then uploads. If an upload fails or you press Ctrl-C, that file is gone from the live site, e.g. `index.html` → homepage 404. | Agree. Worst of the lot, and it hits the live site. |
| **I2** = Entire's finding | The deploy record goes stale after a failed or interrupted run. Rolling back afterwards can report "0 updated" while the newer file stays live. | Agree. |
| **I3** = Entire's hint | `PROT P` (encrypted file transfers) is only checked on the preflight connection. The real upload opens its own connections, which could run in cleartext while the script prints "data connections encrypted". | Agree, but it's unlikely: the server itself would have to behave inconsistently. |
| **I4** | A line in the user's own lftp config such as `set ssl:verify-certificate/<host> no` overrides the script's certificate check. | Agree. It doesn't affect your machine (you have no lftp config file), but it could affect any club member who runs the script. |
| M1 | When a run fails, the summary of what changed is thrown away. | Agree |
| M2 | If the host refuses `SITE CHMOD` (setting file permissions), every `--apply` fails. | Agree |
| M3 | `--delete` has no guard against `FTP_REMOTE_DIR=/`, and could remove files the host manages, like `.htaccess` or `.well-known/`. | Agree. `/` matters here: given the `/www` confusion, the FTP root may hold other folders. |
| M4 | `redact()` would only partly mask a password containing `@`. | **Skip.** lftp writes `@` as `%40` in URLs (`p@ss` came out as `p%40ss` in testing), so a raw `@` never appears. |
| M5 | Test gaps: failed upload followed by rollback, `PROT P` refused on a later connection, Ctrl-C, a server that ignores timestamps, no clear error if the fake server doesn't start. | Agree. Linux testing stays out of scope: no Linux machine here. |
| M6, M7 | The "data connections encrypted" message claims too much, and the docs promise incremental uploads in every case. | Agree. Folded into Tasks 3 and 2. |
| M8 | A server clock running ahead can make lftp skip a file changed shortly after the last upload. | Document only. This is how comparing by timestamp works. |

## Tasks

**Task 1: Never delete a live file before its replacement has uploaded (I1, M2)**
- Add `--overwrite` to the upload, so lftp replaces files in place. Teach the parser lftp's `Overwriting old file` message, so replaced files still count as "updated".
- Add `--no-perms`, so the upload no longer depends on the host allowing `SITE CHMOD`.
- Fake server: new modes that make a chosen upload fail, and that refuse `SITE CHMOD`.
- Tests:
  - A failed upload leaves the old file on the server, and the script exits non-zero.
  - A server that refuses `SITE CHMOD` still deploys fine.

**Task 2: Keep the deploy record correct after a failure (I2, M1, M7)**
- Before a live upload, rewrite the record so it only keeps files whose content hasn't changed. A failed or interrupted run then can't leave stale entries, and unchanged files still aren't re-uploaded.
- On failure, still print the partial summary, with a note: "server may be in a mixed state: re-run, or use `--full`".
- DEPLOYMENT.md: say to use `--full` after deploying from another computer, editing files on the server directly, or a failed run that wasn't fixed by re-running.
- Fake server: new mode that ignores `SITE UTIME` (setting a file's timestamp).
- Tests:
  - Deploy A, then B with one upload failing, then A again: A's files are re-uploaded.
  - On a server that ignores `SITE UTIME`, a rebuild with no changes still uploads nothing.

**Task 3: Check encryption on every upload connection (I3, M6)**
- Turn on lftp's debug log (password masked) for the upload session too. After lftp exits, check it: every connection's `PROT P` must have been accepted. It counts `PROT P` against logins, because replies from parallel connections get mixed up.
- If the check fails: exit non-zero, don't update the deploy record, and print a clear warning to check the site and redeploy.
- This can only detect the problem afterwards. lftp 4.9.3 has no setting to make a refused `PROT P` stop the upload.
- Reword the preflight message to say only what it proved.
- Fake server: new mode that accepts `PROT P` on the first connection only.
- Test: the preflight passes, the check after the upload fails, the exit code is non-zero, and the deploy record is not saved.

**Task 4: Ignore personal lftp settings (I4)**
- Run lftp with `--norc`, so the user's lftp config files are never read.

- `start_server` fails with a clear message if the server doesn't report its port within 5 seconds.
- New Ctrl-C test:
  - A slow-upload mode on the fake server.
  - Send Ctrl-C mid-upload.
  - Expect exit code 130, an unchanged deploy record, no temp files left behind, and no live file missing.

**Task 7: Check and ship**
- Run the full test suite 3 times. For every new fix, break it on purpose and confirm the test fails.
- Commit, push, and resolve Entire's finding with the evidence. Update the PR description.

## Choices to approve (my recommendation first)
1. **I1:** `--overwrite`, as in the plan. The alternative is lftp's `xfer:use-temp-file`: upload under a temporary name, then rename it over the old file. It's safer against a half-written file, but depends on how your host handles renaming over an existing file, which nobody has checked yet. We can revisit it after the first real deploy.
2. **I2:** trim the deploy record to unchanged files, as in the plan. The simpler option deletes the whole record on every live run, which costs one full 20 MB upload after any failure.
3. **Order:** 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7, one commit per task.

Reply "approve", or name the tasks or choices you want changed. I won't touch the code until then.

# Deployment Guide

This guide explains how to deploy the Jyväskylä Cricket Club website.

## Recommended: Netlify Deployment

### Prerequisites
- A GitHub repository with this code
- A Netlify account (free tier is sufficient)

### Steps

1. **Push code to GitHub**
   ```bash
   git add .
   git commit -m "Modernized JCC website with Astro"
   git push origin main
   ```

2. **Connect to Netlify**
   - Go to [https://app.netlify.com](https://app.netlify.com)
   - Click "Add new site" → "Import an existing project"
   - Choose GitHub and select your repository
   - Netlify will auto-detect the Astro framework

3. **Configure Build Settings** (should be auto-detected)
   - Build command: `npm run build`
   - Publish directory: `dist`
   - Node version: 22

4. **Deploy!**
   - Click "Deploy site"
   - Netlify will build and deploy your site
   - You'll get a temporary URL like `random-name.netlify.app`

5. **Custom Domain Setup**
   - Go to Site settings → Domain management
   - Add custom domain: `cricketjyvaskyla.com`
   - Follow DNS configuration instructions
   - Netlify provides free SSL certificates

### Auto-Deploy
After initial setup, every push to `main` branch will automatically:
- Build the site
- Run checks
- Deploy if successful

## Alternative: Vercel Deployment

Similar to Netlify:
1. Go to [https://vercel.com](https://vercel.com)
2. Import your GitHub repository
3. Vercel auto-detects Astro
4. Deploy!

## Alternative: Traditional Hosting

If using traditional hosting (FTP/cPanel):

1. **Build the site locally**
   ```bash
   npm run build
   ```

2. **Upload the `dist/` folder**
   - The `dist/` folder contains all static files
   - Upload contents to your web server's public directory
   - Usually `public_html/` or `www/`

3. **Important**:
   - Ensure PDF files in `dist/pdfs/` are uploaded
   - Check that `robots.txt` and `sitemap.xml` are in root

### Secured upload script (FTPS)

`scripts/deploy-ftp.sh` builds the site and mirrors `dist/` over FTP with mandatory TLS (explicit FTPS, via lftp). It never sends the password unless TLS is negotiated and the server certificate and hostname verify. Before listing or uploading anything, it also checks that the server accepted `PROT P`. Without that, lftp would silently send the files over unencrypted data connections.

One-time setup (macOS):

```bash
brew install lftp
export FTP_USER=<your-ftp-login>
# Store the password in the Keychain. -T "" makes every read ask for approval
# (choose "Allow", never "Always Allow").
security add-generic-password -a "$FTP_USER" -s jcc-ftp -T "" -w
```

Usage:

```bash
export FTP_USER=<your-ftp-login>
export FTP_REMOTE_DIR=/<web-root>      # folder that holds the live site
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh                  # dry run: summary of files that would change
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --apply          # upload
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --apply --delete # also delete remote files not in dist/
scripts/deploy-ftp.sh --full --apply   # re-upload everything
```

- Only files whose content changed since the last successful `--apply` are uploaded. Every build gives every file a new mtime, so the script keeps a record of the last deploy (content hashes and mtimes, in `node_modules/.cache/deploy-ftp/`) and puts back the old mtime on unchanged files. Use `--full` if the server was changed by other means, such as FileZilla.
- Host defaults to `ftps4.us.freehostia.com` (override with `FTP_HOST`).
- Asks for confirmation when not run from `master`.
- Run it in your own terminal, not through an AI agent's shell, so the session transcript never contains deploy output.
- `scripts/test-deploy-ftp.sh` is an offline end-to-end test. It runs the real script against a local fake FTPS server (`scripts/fake_ftps_server.py`) that uses a throwaway test CA, and needs python3, lftp, openssl and node.
  - Refusal cases: the server refuses TLS, presents an untrusted certificate, rejects `PROT P`, or the password is wrong. The test checks that nothing is uploaded and the password is never sent or printed.
  - Success cases: it checks the summary and the server contents for a dry run, `--delete`, `--apply`, a rebuild with no changes, a single changed file, a German locale and `--full`.

- FileZilla: use host `ftps4.us.freehostia.com` with "Require explicit FTP over TLS". Plain FTP sends the password unencrypted.

## Environment Variables

No environment variables needed for basic deployment. All configuration is in `astro.config.mjs`.

## Post-Deployment Checklist

- [ ] Site loads at custom domain
- [ ] All 8 pages are accessible
- [ ] Images load correctly
- [ ] PDFs download properly
- [ ] Navigation works on mobile
- [ ] SSL certificate active (HTTPS)
- [ ] robots.txt accessible at `/robots.txt`
- [ ] sitemap.xml accessible at `/sitemap.xml`
- [ ] Old URLs redirect to new ones (e.g., `/members.html` → `/members`)

## Monitoring

- **Netlify**: Built-in analytics available
- **Google Search Console**: Add your domain for SEO monitoring
- **Google Analytics**: Add tracking code if needed

## Rollback

If you need to rollback:
- **Netlify**: Go to Deploys → select previous deploy → "Publish deploy"
- **Vercel**: Similar rollback in deployments section

## Support

For issues:
- Netlify docs: https://docs.netlify.com
- Astro docs: https://docs.astro.build
- Contact: chairman@cricketjyvaskyla.com

4	//
5	// After a successful deploy, `save` records each file's SHA-256 and mtime.
6	// Before the next deploy, `restore` gives every file whose content is

8	// newer than the server's copy.
9	//

20	  console.error('usage: deploy-ftp-state.mjs restore|save <distDir> <manifest.json>');
21	  process.exit(2);
22	}
23	
24	function* walk(dir) {
25	  for (const entry of readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true })) {
26	    const full = join(dir, entry.name);
27	    if (entry.isDirectory()) yield* walk(full);
28	    else if (entry.isFile()) yield full;
29	  }
30	}

32	const sha256 = (file) => createHash('sha256').update(readFileSync(file)).digest('hex');
33	const key = (file) => relative(distDir, file).split(sep).join('/');

Base directory for this skill: /Users/akshay.guleria/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/superpowers/7.0.2/skills/requesting-code-review

# Requesting Code Review

Dispatch a code reviewer subagent to catch issues before they cascade. The reviewer gets precisely crafted context for evaluation — never your session's history.

**Core principle:** Review early, review often.

## When to Request Review

**Mandatory:**
- After each task in subagent-driven development
- After completing major feature
- Before merge to main

**Optional but valuable:**
- When stuck (fresh perspective)
- Before refactoring (baseline check)
- After fixing complex bug

## How to Request

**1. Get git SHAs:**
```bash
BASE_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD~1)  # or: git merge-base origin/main HEAD
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
```

**2. Dispatch code reviewer subagent:**

Dispatch a `general-purpose` subagent, filling the template at [code-reviewer.md](code-reviewer.md)

**Placeholders:**
- `{DESCRIPTION}` - Brief summary of what you built
- `{PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS}` - What it should do
- `{BASE_SHA}` - Starting commit
- `{HEAD_SHA}` - Ending commit

**3. Act on feedback:**
- Fix Critical issues immediately
- Fix Important issues before proceeding
- Note Minor issues for later
- Push back if reviewer is wrong (with reasoning)

## Example

```
[Just completed Task 2: Add verification function]

You: Let me request code review before proceeding.

BASE_SHA=$(git log --oneline | grep "Task 1" | head -1 | cut -d' ' -f1)
HEAD_SHA=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

[Dispatch code reviewer subagent]
  DESCRIPTION: Added verifyIndex() and repairIndex() with 4 issue types
  PLAN_OR_REQUIREMENTS: Task 2 from docs/superpowers/plans/deployment-plan.md
  BASE_SHA: a7981ec
  HEAD_SHA: 3df7661

[Subagent returns]:
  Strengths: Clean architecture, real tests
  Issues:
    Important: Missing progress indicators
    Minor: Magic number (100) for reporting interval
  Assessment: Ready to proceed

You: [Fix progress indicators]
[Continue to Task 3]
```

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I'll just review the diff myself instead of dispatching a reviewer" | You're the coordinator — reviewing the diff inline burns the context window you need to keep driving the work. Dispatch a reviewer subagent: the diff and the evaluation live in its context, and only the findings come back to you. |
| "The reviewer needs my whole session history to understand the change" | Hand it precisely crafted context, never your session's history. That keeps the reviewer on the work product, not your thought process. |

## Red Flags

**Never:**
- Skip review because "it's simple"
- Ignore Critical issues
- Proceed with unfixed Important issues
- Argue with valid technical feedback

**If reviewer wrong:**
- Push back with technical reasoning
- Show code/tests that prove it works
- Request clarification

See template at: [code-reviewer.md](code-reviewer.md)


ARGUMENTS: review the above issues, structure the fixes into tasks. Wait for my approval before implementation

Understand the project's security model and threat model Phase 2 - Comparative Analysis: - Compare new code changes against existing security patterns - Identify deviations from established secure practices - Look for inconsistent security implementations - Flag code that introduces new attack surfaces Phase 3 - Vulnerability Assessment: - Examine each modified file for security implications - Trace data flow from user inputs to sensitive operations - Look for privilege boundaries being crossed unsafely - Identify injection points and unsafe deserialization REQUIRED OUTPUT FORMAT: You MUST output your findings in markdown. The markdown output should contain the file, line number, severity, category (e.g. `sql_injection` or `xss`), description, exploit scenario, and fix recommendation. For example: # Vuln 1: XSS: `foo.py:42` * Severity: High * Description: User input from `username` parameter is directly interpolated into HTML without escaping, allowing reflected XSS attacks * Exploit Scenario: Attacker crafts URL like /bar?q= to execute JavaScript in victim's browser, enabling session hijacking or data theft * Recommendation: Use Flask's escape() function or Jinja2 templates with auto-escaping enabled for all user inputs rendered in HTML SEVERITY GUIDELINES: - **HIGH**: Directly exploitable vulnerabilities leading to RCE, data breach, or authentication bypass - **MEDIUM**: Vulnerabilities requiring specific conditions but with significant impact - **LOW**: Defense-in-depth issues or lower-impact vulnerabilities CONFIDENCE SCORING: - 0.9-1.0: Certain exploit path identified, tested if possible - 0.8-0.9: Clear vulnerability pattern with known exploitation methods - 0.7-0.8: Suspicious pattern requiring specific conditions to exploit - Below 0.7: Don't report (too speculative) FINAL REMINDER: Focus on HIGH and MEDIUM findings only. Better to miss some theoretical issues than flood the report with false positives. Each finding should be something a security engineer would confidently raise in a PR review. FALSE POSITIVE FILTERING: > You do not need to run commands to reproduce the vulnerability, just read the code to determine if it is a real vulnerability. Do not use the bash tool or write to any files. > > HARD EXCLUSIONS - Automatically exclude findings matching these patterns: > 1. Denial of Service (DOS) vulnerabilities or resource exhaustion attacks. > 2. Secrets or credentials stored on disk if they are otherwise secured. > 3. Rate limiting concerns or service overload scenarios. > 4. Memory consumption or CPU exhaustion issues. > 5. Lack of input validation on non-security-critical fields without proven security impact. > 6. Input sanitization concerns for GitHub Action workflows unless they are clearly triggerable via untrusted input. > 7. A lack of hardening measures. Code is not expected to implement all security best practices, only flag concrete vulnerabilities. > 8. Race conditions or timing attacks that are theoretical rather than practical issues. Only report a race condition if it is concretely problematic. > 9. Vulnerabilities related to outdated third-party libraries. These are managed separately and should not be reported here. > 10. Memory safety issues such as buffer overflows or use-after-free-vulnerabilities are impossible in rust. Do not report memory safety issues in rust or any other memory safe languages. > 11. Files that are only unit tests or only used as part of running tests. > 12. Log spoofing concerns. Outputting un-sanitized user input to logs is not a vulnerability. > 13. SSRF vulnerabilities that only control the path. SSRF is only a concern if it can control the host or protocol. > 14. Including user-controlled content in AI system prompts is not a vulnerability. > 15. Regex injection. Injecting untrusted content into a regex is not a vulnerability. > 16. Regex DOS concerns. > 16. Insecure documentation. Do not report any findings in documentation files such as markdown files. > 17. A lack of audit logs is not a vulnerability. > > PRECEDENTS - > 1. Logging high value secrets in plaintext is a vulnerability. Logging URLs is assumed to be safe. > 2. UUIDs can be assumed to be unguessable and do not need to be validated. > 3. Environment variables and CLI flags are trusted values. Attackers are generally not able to modify them in a secure environment. Any attack that relies on controlling an environment variable is invalid. > 4. Resource management issues such as memory or file descriptor leaks are not valid. > 5. Subtle or low impact web vulnerabilities such as tabnabbing, XS-Leaks, prototype pollution, and open redirects should not be reported unless they are extremely high confidence. > 6. React and Angular are generally secure against XSS. These frameworks do not need to sanitize or escape user input unless it is using dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrustHtml, or similar methods. Do not report XSS vulnerabilities in React or Angular components or tsx files unless they are using unsafe methods. > 7. Most vulnerabilities in github action workflows are not exploitable in practice. Before validating a github action workflow vulnerability ensure it is concrete and has a very specific attack path. > 8. A lack of permission checking or authentication in client-side JS/TS code is not a vulnerability. Client-side code is not trusted and does not need to implement these checks, they are handled on the server-side. The same applies to all flows that send untrusted data to the backend, the backend is responsible for validating and sanitizing all inputs. > 9. Only include MEDIUM findings if they are obvious and concrete issues. > 10. Most vulnerabilities in ipython notebooks (*.ipynb files) are not exploitable in practice. Before validating a notebook vulnerability ensure it is concrete and has a very specific attack path where untrusted input can trigger the vulnerability. > 11. Logging non-PII data is not a vulnerability even if the data may be sensitive. Only report logging vulnerabilities if they expose sensitive information such as secrets, passwords, or personally identifiable information (PII). > 12. Command injection vulnerabilities in shell scripts are generally not exploitable in practice since shell scripts generally do not run with untrusted user input. Only report command injection vulnerabilities in shell scripts if they are concrete and have a very specific attack path for untrusted input. > > SIGNAL QUALITY CRITERIA - For remaining findings, assess: > 1. Is there a concrete, exploitable vulnerability with a clear attack path? > 2. Does this represent a real security risk vs theoretical best practice? > 3. Are there specific code locations and reproduction steps? > 4. Would this finding be actionable for a security team? > > For each finding, assign a confidence score from 1-10: > - 1-3: Low confidence, likely false positive or noise > - 4-6: Medium confidence, needs investigation > - 7-10: High confidence, likely true vulnerability START ANALYSIS: Begin your analysis now. Do this in 3 steps: 1. Use a sub-task to identify vulnerabilities. Use the repository exploration tools to understand the codebase context, then analyze the PR changes for security implications. In the prompt for this sub-task, include all of the above. 2. Then for each vulnerability identified by the above sub-task, create a new sub-task to filter out false-positives. Launch these sub-tasks as parallel sub-tasks. In the prompt for these sub-tasks, include everything in the "FALSE POSITIVE FILTERING" instructions. 3. Filter out any vulnerabilities where the sub-task reported a confidence less than 8. Your final reply must contain the markdown report and nothing else.

This is not a general code review - focus ONLY on security implications newly added by this PR. Do not comment on existing security concerns. CRITICAL INSTRUCTIONS: 1. MINIMIZE FALSE POSITIVES: Only flag issues where you're >80% confident of actual exploitability 2. AVOID NOISE: Skip theoretical issues, style concerns, or low-impact findings 3. FOCUS ON IMPACT: Prioritize vulnerabilities that could lead to unauthorized access, data breaches, or system compromise 4. EXCLUSIONS: Do NOT report the following issue types: - Denial of Service (DOS) vulnerabilities, even if they allow service disruption - Secrets or sensitive data stored on disk (these are handled by other processes) - Rate limiting or resource exhaustion issues SECURITY CATEGORIES TO EXAMINE: **Input Validation Vulnerabilities:** - SQL injection via unsanitized user input - Command injection in system calls or subprocesses - XXE injection in XML parsing - Template injection in templating engines - NoSQL injection in database queries - Path traversal in file operations **Authentication & Authorization Issues:** - Authentication bypass logic - Privilege escalation paths - Session management flaws - JWT token vulnerabilities - Authorization logic bypasses **Crypto & Secrets Management:** - Hardcoded API keys, passwords, or tokens - Weak cryptographic algorithms or implementations - Improper key storage or management - Cryptographic randomness issues - Certificate validation bypasses **Injection & Code Execution:** - Remote code execution via deseralization - Pickle injection in Python - YAML deserialization vulnerabilities - Eval injection in dynamic code execution - XSS vulnerabilities in web applications (reflected, stored, DOM-based) **Data Exposure:** - Sensitive data logging or storage - PII handling violations - API endpoint data leakage - Debug information exposure Additional notes: - Even if something is only exploitable from the local network, it can still be a HIGH severity issue ANALYSIS METHODOLOGY: Phase 1 - Repository Context Research (Use file search tools): - Identify existing security frameworks and libraries in use - Look for established secure coding patterns in the codebase - Examine existing sanitization and validation patterns - Understand the project's security model and threat model Phase 2 - Comparative Analysis: - Compare new code changes against existing security patterns - Identify deviations from established secure practices - Look for inconsistent security implementations - Flag code that introduces new attack surfaces Phase 3 - Vulnerability Assessment: - Examine each modified file for security implications - Trace data flow from user inputs to sensitive operations - Look for privilege boundaries being crossed unsafely - Identify injection points and unsafe deserialization REQUIRED OUTPUT FORMAT: You MUST output your findings in markdown. The markdown output should contain the file, line number, severity, category (e.g. `sql_injection` or `xss`), description, exploit scenario, and fix recommendation. For example: # Vuln 1: XSS: `foo.py:42` * Severity: High * Description: User input from `username` parameter is directly interpolated into HTML without escaping, allowing reflected XSS attacks * Exploit Scenario: Attacker crafts URL like /bar?q= to execute JavaScript in victim's browser, enabling session hijacking or data theft * Recommendation: Use Flask's escape() function or Jinja2 templates with auto-escaping enabled for all user inputs rendered in HTML SEVERITY GUIDELINES: - **HIGH**: Directly exploitable vulnerabilities leading to RCE, data breach, or authentication bypass - **MEDIUM**: Vulnerabilities requiring specific conditions but with significant impact - **LOW**: Defense-in-depth issues or lower-impact vulnerabilities CONFIDENCE SCORING: - 0.9-1.0: Certain exploit path identified, tested if possible - 0.8-0.9: Clear vulnerability pattern with known exploitation methods - 0.7-0.8: Suspicious pattern requiring specific conditions to exploit - Below 0.7: Don't report (too speculative) FINAL REMINDER: Focus on HIGH and MEDIUM findings only. Better to miss some theoretical issues than flood the report with false positives. Each finding should be something a security engineer would confidently raise in a PR review. FALSE POSITIVE FILTERING: > You do not need to run commands to reproduce the vulnerability, just read the code to determine if it is a real vulnerability. Do not use the bash tool or write to any files. > > HARD EXCLUSIONS - Automatically exclude findings matching these patterns: > 1. Denial of Service (DOS) vulnerabilities or resource exhaustion attacks. > 2. Secrets or credentials stored on disk if they are otherwise secured. > 3. Rate limiting concerns or service overload scenarios. > 4. Memory consumption or CPU exhaustion issues. > 5. Lack of input validation on non-security-critical fields without proven security impact. > 6. Input sanitization concerns for GitHub Action workflows unless they are clearly triggerable via untrusted input. > 7. A lack of hardening measures. Code is not expected to implement all security best practices, only flag concrete vulnerabilities. > 8. Race conditions or timing attacks that are theoretical rather than practical issues. Only report a race condition if it is concretely problematic. > 9. Vulnerabilities related to outdated third-party libraries. These are managed separately and should not be reported here. > 10. Memory safety issues such as buffer overflows or use-after-free-vulnerabilities are impossible in rust. Do not report memory safety issues in rust or any other memory safe languages. > 11. Files that are only unit tests or only used as part of running tests. > 12. Log spoofing concerns. Outputting un-sanitized user input to logs is not a vulnerability. > 13. SSRF vulnerabilities that only control the path. SSRF is only a concern if it can control the host or protocol. > 14. Including user-controlled content in AI system prompts is not a vulnerability. > 15. Regex injection. Injecting untrusted content into a regex is not a vulnerability. > 16. Regex DOS concerns. > 16. Insecure documentation. Do not report any findings in documentation files such as markdown files. > 17. A lack of audit logs is not a vulnerability. > > PRECEDENTS - > 1. Logging high value secrets in plaintext is a vulnerability. Logging URLs is assumed to be safe. > 2. UUIDs can be assumed to be unguessable and do not need to be validated. > 3. Environment variables and CLI flags are trusted values. Attackers are generally not able to modify them in a secure environment. Any attack that relies on controlling an environment variable is invalid. > 4. Resource management issues such as memory or file descriptor leaks are not valid. > 5. Subtle or low impact web vulnerabilities such as tabnabbing, XS-Leaks, prototype pollution, and open redirects should not be reported unless they are extremely high confidence. > 6. React and Angular are generally secure against XSS. These frameworks do not need to sanitize or escape user input unless it is using dangerouslySetInnerHTML, bypassSecurityTrustHtml, or similar methods. Do not report XSS vulnerabilities in React or Angular components or tsx files unless they are using unsafe methods. > 7. Most vulnerabilities in github action workflows are not exploitable in practice. Before validating a github action workflow vulnerability ensure it is concrete and has a very specific attack path. > 8. A lack of permission checking or authentication in client-side JS/TS code is not a vulnerability. Client-side code is not trusted and does not need to implement these checks, they are handled on the server-side. The same applies to all flows that send untrusted data to the backend, the backend is responsible for validating and sanitizing all inputs. > 9. Only include MEDIUM findings if they are obvious and concrete issues. > 10. Most vulnerabilities in ipython notebooks (*.ipynb files) are not exploitable in practice. Before validating a notebook vulnerability ensure it is concrete and has a very specific attack path where untrusted input can trigger the vulnerability. > 11. Logging non-PII data is not a vulnerability even if the data may be sensitive. Only report logging vulnerabilities if they expose sensitive information such as secrets, passwords, or personally identifiable information (PII). > 12. Command injection vulnerabilities in shell scripts are generally not exploitable in practice since shell scripts generally do not run with untrusted user input. Only report command injection vulnerabilities in shell scripts if they are concrete and have a very specific attack path for untrusted input. > > SIGNAL QUALITY CRITERIA - For remaining findings, assess: > 1. Is there a concrete, exploitable vulnerability with a clear attack path? > 2. Does this represent a real security risk vs theoretical best practice? > 3. Are there specific code locations and reproduction steps? > 4. Would this finding be actionable for a security team? > > For each finding, assign a confidence score from 1-10: > - 1-3: Low confidence, likely false positive or noise > - 4-6: Medium confidence, needs investigation > - 7-10: High confidence, likely true vulnerability START ANALYSIS: Begin your analysis now. Do this in 3 steps: 1. Use a sub-task to identify vulnerabilities. Use the repository exploration tools to understand the codebase context, then analyze the PR changes for security implications. In the prompt for this sub-task, include all of the above. 2. Then for each vulnerability identified by the above sub-task, create a new sub-task to filter out false-positives. Launch these sub-tasks as parallel sub-tasks. In the prompt for these sub-tasks, include everything in the "FALSE POSITIVE FILTERING" instructions. 3. Filter out any vulnerabilities where the sub-task reported a confidence less than 8. Your final reply must contain the markdown report and nothing else.
